# Cattail Run Data Campus — Phase 1 foundation strategy: spread footings versus aggregate piers

## Situation

Ardent Vale Infrastructure LLC is building six single-storey building pads (`CR-P1` … `CR-P6`) on
the Cattail Run Data Campus in Loudoun County, Virginia. You are the structural engineer of record
for the Phase 1 foundation package. The data room is under `project/`:

* `criteria/` — the governing geotechnical, structural and concrete criteria and guide
  specifications, together with cancelled predecessor volumes you must recognise and set aside;
* `references/` — the analysis manuals the criteria point to for bearing capacity, settlement,
  lateral earth pressure and sliding, reinforced-concrete footing design, and ground modification,
  plus one manual written for a different class of structure;
* `geotech/` — the geotechnical data report, two boring logs per pad, the laboratory summary, a
  superseded addendum, an adjacent-parcel report, and, in `geotech/regional/`, real regional soil
  and climate data products;
* `structural/` — the base-reaction force vectors exported from the analytical model, the column
  grid, and the load-combination memorandum;
* `civil/` — the grading and groundwater record;
* `cost/` — the contractor bid schedule and the ground-improvement subcontractor's budget proposal;
* `owner/` — the basis of design (and its superseded revision), the authority-having-jurisdiction
  amendment letter, the RFI log, the BIM parameter standard and the schedule and register templates.

Every parameter is found in those documents. **None of them is restated here.**

Each pad carries one instrumented column line of six foundation units: five isolated column
footings and one continuous shear-wall footing. For every one of the thirty-six foundations you must
size the footing, set the reinforcement, assign the concrete, and decide whether it is carried on a
shallow spread footing alone or on a spread footing over rammed aggregate piers. All foundations on
a pad share one bearing elevation. Ground improvement is bought by the rig, not by the pad, and the
subcontractor's mobilisation and scheduling terms constrain how many pads one mobilised rig can
serve. The campus programme must be compliant at every foundation and **should cost as little as
possible** at the project unit prices.

The unit prices issued with the basis of design are project budget prices prepared for this
procurement. They are fictional for any other purpose; optimise against them as issued.

## Deliverable

A single file **`output/submission.zip`** containing exactly these six files at the archive root:

1. **`foundation_geometry.json`** — the Revit foundation geometry parameter file, in the shape and
   with the rules the owner's BIM parameter standard sets out. It is what the grader parses: every
   number in it is yours, derived from the documents.

2. **`ground_improvement_plan.json`** — the ground-improvement programme, in the shape the same BIM
   parameter standard sets out: the stress concentration ratio and pier diameter adopted, the rigs
   mobilised with the pads each one serves, the mobilisation cost, the verification-testing count
   per improved pad, and per improved pad the stiffness modulus used, the treatment depth and the
   total pier linear feet.

3. **`foundation_schedule.xlsx`** — the foundation schedule, on the owner's template, one row per
   foundation for all thirty-six, with the columns the template defines. It must agree with the
   parameter file.

4. **`foundation_feasibility_matrix.md`** — the foundation-type feasibility and optimisation matrix.
   For every pad (headed by its pad ID) and every foundation on it: the demand, the bearing check,
   the predicted settlement, the stability checks on the shear-wall footing, the constraint that
   governs, and the shallow-versus-improved decision with the cost of **both** alternatives that
   decided it.

5. **`constraint_register.xlsx`** — the register of every requirement you applied, on the owner's
   template, with the columns `req_id`, `document`, `clause`, `requirement`, `value`, `unit`,
   `kind`, `applies_to`, `resolution`. The register is scored. Register what you actually used, with
   the real document and the real clause, table or equation number. A requirement family whose
   governing clause you did not register earns no credit even if your numbers are right. Only the
   first **96 rows** are read for matching, so putting the substance first matters. Rows that cite a
   document which is not in the data room at all, and rows that cite a cancelled or superseded
   document as if it were live, reduce the register's credit; a row that cites a cancelled or
   superseded document and says in its `resolution` column that it was set aside is neutral, and so
   is any additional correct row. A register whose credit falls below 0.30 is treated as padding and
   registers nothing at all; below a credit of 0.60 the register score is scaled down in proportion.

6. **`design_basis.md`** — the design basis. It must **open with a fenced ` ```json ` block** of
   this shape, followed by the narrative:

   ```json
   {"frost": {"afi_100yr_F_days": 0, "afi_product_period": "...", "frost_depth_in": 0,
              "superseded_product_period": "...", "superseded_afi_100yr_F_days": 0},
    "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {"governing_constraint": "...",
                          "foundation_decision": "SPREAD|IMPROVED_SPREAD",
                          "spread_only_cost_usd": 0, "improved_cost_usd": 0}},
    "campus": {"rigs_mobilised": 0, "mobilisation_cost_usd": 0, "total_cost_usd": 0,
               "pads_improved": ["..."]},
    "rejected_criteria": ["..."]}
   ```

   The narrative must state: the criteria that govern and the documents that were reviewed and set
   aside, with the reason; the bearing-capacity and settlement methods actually applied and the
   basis of the factor of safety used at each pad; the tolerable-movement criteria adopted and any
   competing criterion rejected; the ground-improvement design parameters with the authority for
   each; how every conflict between documents was resolved, with the governing value; and the
   reasoning behind the campus programme — which pads are improved, how many rigs are mobilised and
   why that number.

Keep the archive under 25 MB and 200 files.

## Grading

Pads are graded individually against the grader's own derivation from the same documents; a subset
of the pads is used for scoring. Requirement families are tagged HARD (bearing capacity and the
factor of safety, the groundwater correction, the bearing stratum, total and differential
settlement, minimum widths, frost protection, sliding, overturning and uplift of the shear-wall
footing, footing shear and reinforcement, the sulfate exposure condition and the concrete durability
limits, the aggregate-pier replacement ratio, stress ratio, stiffness modulus and treatment depth,
the mobilisation programme, and the prohibition on presumptive bearing values) or SOFT (schedule
completeness, parameter-file conformance, the verification-testing programme, and the design-basis
statements — four of which are judged by an LLM against verbatim quotes from `design_basis.md`).

### How your reported analysis values are reviewed

The grader re-derives the physics from **your own geometry** and checks that your design is safe.
Where it also compares a number you *reported*, the comparison is **one-sided and tolerant of
conservatism** — being more cautious than the grader's recomputation never costs you a family:

* a **capacity** you report may not be more permissive than the grader's recomputation by more than
  **6 %** (net allowable bearing pressure; sliding and uplift factors of safety, 20 %). Any bearing
  method at least as conservative as the general bearing-capacity equation of the governing
  foundations manual is accepted — including the least of three methods. There is **no lower bound**
  on a reported capacity;
* a **demand** you report may not fall below the grader's recomputation by more than **15 %**
  (applied net bearing pressure), **20 %** (settlement, eccentricity), **10 %** (top-of-pier
  stress). There is **no upper bound**;
* the recomputed **angular distortion between adjacent units** is graded against the criteria's own
  limit **exactly**. Both sides of that comparison are computed by the grader from your geometry
  with the settlement procedure the data room states, so no reporting band applies to it;
* required **flexural steel** is a lower bound with a **10 %** tolerance; the code minimum
  reinforcement ratios are exact;
* the recomputed **shear thickness** requirement is a lower bound evaluated with the most permissive
  strength-reduction factor in general use, so a footing designed by the shipped manual's own worked
  examples is thicker than required;
* the one-sided bands have a **sanity floor**: a reported net allowable bearing pressure may not
  fall below **half** the grader's recomputation (the least of three widely accepted methods is
  about 0.82 × of it, so the floor is more than three times clear of the most conservative method
  the criteria invite), and a reported settlement may not exceed the total-settlement limit you are
  designing to. Neither test costs a conservative solver anything;
* the **hard limits themselves are exact**: the total-settlement limit, the minimum footing widths,
  the minimum factors of safety, the exposure classes and the concrete limits, the
  replacement-ratio, top-of-pier-stress and treatment-depth bounds, and the owner's dimensioning
  grid and minimum footing thickness.

The governing constraint you name for a pad is accepted if it is a constraint that **selects** that
pad's design: either taking one 3-in step of plan width off any one foundation on the pad (with that
footing's shear thickness re-derived at the smaller width) would violate it, or your **own reported**
bearing, settlement or differential-settlement numbers put it at **80 %** or more of its limit
somewhere on the pad. Footing thickness and bearing elevation are dependent variables of this
problem - the thickness follows from shear and the elevation from frost - so `PUNCHING_SHEAR` is not
a pad-level governing constraint, and `FROST` is accepted only where the pad is founded at the frost
minimum and nothing else on it is near binding. All nine values remain legal per foundation in the
parameter file.

Per pad: a family earns credit only if it is **both** satisfied **and** registered. Let `p` be
the fraction of all 32 families satisfied-and-registered, multiplied by the register precision factor
described above, and `h` the fraction of the 22 HARD families satisfied-and-registered (not multiplied
by that factor). Let `O` be the programme credit = (a certified lower
bound on the cost of any compliant campus programme) / (the grader's repricing of **your** design
at the project unit prices), capped at 1.

The pad score is `0.4 p + 0.6 [h = 1] O'`, where `O' = clip((O - O_naive) / (1 - O_naive), 0, 1)` and
`O_naive` is the programme credit of a naive baseline programme. Thus a parseable pad earns programme
credit (none when the design cannot be repriced) only when all of its HARD families are
satisfied-and-registered (`h = 1`): an omitted citation or a physical
HARD violation forfeits the programme credit. A missing or
unparseable pad scores 0. The task score is the mean over the graded pads.

The lower bound comes from a relaxation of the campus problem, so the programme credit is strictly
below 1 for every attainable design; a cheaper compliant programme never scores worse than a more
expensive one, and the grader reprices your own decisions, so a programme that under-buys
mobilisations or misstates a quantity is repriced at what it actually costs. Reinforcement is priced
at the greater of the ratio you report and the ratio your design actually requires, so the tolerance
on the flexural steel cannot be spent on cost.

# Cattail Run Data Campus - BIM foundation parameter standard (Rev. 2)

The foundation geometry parameter file is consumed directly by the Revit family generator.  It is a
single UTF-8 JSON object named `foundation_geometry.json` with this shape:

```json
{"project": {"campus_total_cost_usd": 0.0, "frost_depth_in": 0, "afi_100yr_F_days": 0},
 "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {
     "bearing_depth_in": 0, "fs_bearing": 0.0, "occupancy_class": "...",
     "improved": false, "sulfate_pct": 0.0, "sulfate_exposure_class": "S0|S1|S2",
     "exposure_classes": ["..."], "fc_psi": 0, "max_wcm": 0.0, "dewatering_days": 0,
     "governing_constraint": "...",
     "foundations": {"<TAG>": {
         "foundation_type": "SPREAD|IMPROVED_SPREAD",
         "B_in": 0, "L_in": 0, "thickness_in": 0, "bearing_stratum": "I|II|III",
         "reinforcement_ratio": 0.0, "bar_size": 4, "bar_spacing_in": 12,
         "q_net_ksf": 0.0, "q_allow_net_ksf": 0.0, "settlement_in": 0.0,
         "pier_count": 0, "pier_diameter_in": 0, "pier_depth_ft": 0,
         "area_replacement_ratio": 0.0, "top_of_pier_stress_psf": 0.0,
         "governing_constraint": "..."}}}}}
```

Rules the generator enforces:

* every one of the six pads and every one of its six foundations must be present;
* `B_in`, `L_in`, `thickness_in` and `bearing_depth_in` are NUMBERS in inches, dimensioned to the
  nearest 3 in; `pier_depth_ft` is a whole number of feet; `pier_count` is a whole number;
* no `null` values anywhere; a spread footing carries zeros in the pier fields;
* `bearing_depth_in` is identical for every foundation on a pad and is repeated once at pad level;
* `governing_constraint` is one of `BEARING`, `SETTLEMENT`, `ANGULAR_DISTORTION`, `MIN_WIDTH`,
  `SLIDING`, `OVERTURNING`, `UPLIFT`, `PUNCHING_SHEAR`, `FROST`;
* the shear-wall foundation of each pad additionally carries `sliding_fs`, `eccentricity_in` and
  `uplift_fs`.

The ground-improvement plan is a separate JSON object named `ground_improvement_plan.json`:

```json
{"stress_concentration_ratio_ns": 0.0, "pier_diameter_in": 0,
 "rigs_mobilised": 0, "mobilisation_cost_usd": 0.0, "pads_improved": ["..."],
 "rig_assignments": {"RIG-1": ["<PAD-ID>", "..."]},
 "modulus_tests": {"<PAD-ID>": 0},
 "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {"stiffness_modulus_pci": 0.0, "treatment_depth_ft": 0,
                       "total_pier_lf": 0.0}}}
```

`treatment_depth_ft` at pad level is the deepest treatment depth used on that pad.

Basis of Design - Structural - Cattail Run Data Campus (Rev. 3)
1. Project
This revision supersedes Revision 1 of this basis of design in its entirety.  Revision 1 is retained for record only.
Ardent Vale Infrastructure LLC is developing the Cattail Run Data Campus in Loudoun County, Virginia.  Six single-storey building pads are in Phase 1.  This basis of design governs the foundation design for all six.
2. Occupancy classification and exposure classes
The occupancy classification below is the STRUCTURE row that applies to each building when a minimum factor of safety on bearing is selected from the geotechnical criteria.  The freezing-and-thawing, water and corrosion exposure classes are assigned by the owner for the foundation concrete of each building.  The SULFATE exposure class is NOT assigned here: it must be established from the measured water-soluble sulfate concentration of the Stratum I soils at each pad.
Foundation concrete of the Logistics and Spares Warehouse supports the exterior loading apron and is exposed to de-icing chemicals, which is why its freezing-and-thawing exposure class is more severe than the other pads.
3. Concrete
The maximum water-cementitious materials ratio and the minimum specified compressive strength for each pad are the most restrictive of the requirements for every exposure class assigned to that pad.  Only the strengths listed in the bid schedule are available from the plant serving this site; specify the lowest listed strength that satisfies both durability and structural demand.
Grade 60 reinforcement, fy = 60,000 psi.  The project minimum reinforcement ratio for shrinkage and temperature in a footing is 0.0018 in each direction; where the governing criteria impose a higher minimum for thick footings, that minimum governs.  Concrete cover to the bottom mat is 3 in plus one bar diameter; take the effective depth as the thickness less 4 in.
For quantity take-off and for the self-weight of a footing, take the unit weight of reinforced concrete as 150 pcf and the unit weight of reinforcing steel as 490 pcf.  Reinforcement is placed in two directions; the pay quantity of reinforcing steel in a footing is twice the reinforcement ratio times the gross footing volume times the unit weight of steel.
4. Dimensioning and deliverable conventions
Footing plan dimensions and thickness are dimensioned to the nearest 3 in.  Foundation bearing depths below finished grade are dimensioned to the nearest 3 in and shall not exceed 15 ft.  All foundations on a building pad share a single bearing elevation.
No footing on this project is thinner than 12 in, whatever the structural calculation returns.
Pier counts are whole piers and treatment depths are whole feet.
5. Cost basis
The unit prices issued with this basis of design are PROJECT BUDGET PRICES prepared for this procurement.  They are fictional for any other purpose and are not published market data.  The campus foundation programme is to be optimised against them.

4.2.2   Design Procedures

Rammed aggregate piers are typically selected to increase bearing resistance, reduce
settlement, increase shear strength, or provide any combination of the above.

Preliminary design methods and assumptions to achieve the desired end result are outlined in
this section.

The generalized design process for an embankment support is as follows:

   1. Perform embankment design without rammed aggregate piers to determine the overall
      settlement and global stability to determine if rammed aggregate piers or another
      form of ground improvement are required. If so proceed to step 2.
   2. Assume an area replacement ratio and column diameter.
   3. Determine the spacing based on the assumed area replacement ratio and column
      diameter.
   4. Check the load bearing resistance of the rammed aggregate pier to see if it meets the
      project requirements. If not revise the column diameter and re-check.
   5. Determine the total settlement of the embankment supported on rammed aggregate
      piers.

As indicated by Figure 5-3(d), the general shear mechanism applies mostly to dense
soils at relatively shallow depths. At lower relative densities and greater footing depths,
the failure mode transitions through local failure to punching shear. The bearing
capacity theories discussed in Section 5-3.1.2 assume a general shear failure
mechanism. Methods to account for local shear are discussed in Section 5-3.1.3.

5-3.1.1       Shear Strength for Bearing Capacity Analysis.

Bearing capacity is controlled by the shear strength of the soil. The type of shear
strength parameters used in bearing capacity analyses depends on the field loading
condition, soil type, and groundwater level. Loads are typically applied to foundations
over a period of time, such as when a building or a bridge is under construction. This
loading condition may represent drained or undrained loading depending on the type of
soil being loaded and the length of time required to apply the load.

In clean sands and gravels, drainage is almost instantaneous and does not practically
depend on how long it takes to build the structure. These soils only require effective
stress analysis unless dynamic loading is anticipated. If substantial fines are present,
the possibility of developing an undrained condition should be considered.

In contrast, substantial time is required for excess pore pressures to dissipate in fine-
grained soils after loading. These soils usually require undrained analysis for conditions
at the end of loading as well as for any rapid or dynamic loading. In some cases, long-
term effective stress conditions should also be checked. For example, the drained
bearing capacity of heavily overconsolidated clays often controls the design.

Laboratory and field testing methods to determine shear strength parameters for most
soil types are summarized in the Prologue. For bearing capacity analysis, effective
strength parameters (φ ʹ, cʹ) should be used for long-term conditions in all soil types. For
saturated fine-grained soils, the use of undrained shear strength (su) with φ = 0 is
appropriate. Undrained shear strength parameters (φ, c) should be used for unsaturated
soils with low permeability, including coarse-grained soils with substantial fines.

5-3.1.2       Calculation of Ultimate Bearing Capacity.

Bearing capacity is a complex phenomenon that cannot be modeled exactly. Multiple
equations have been developed to estimate the ultimate bearing capacity of soil. These
equations are based on the upper and lower bound theorems of plasticity and include

                                            285
                                                                           UFC 3-220-20
                                                                       16 January 2025


the work of Prandtl (1920), Terzaghi (1943), Meyerhof (1951), Brinch Hansen (1970),
and Vesic (1973, 1975). In their basic form, the equations apply to general shear failure
below a continuous strip footing of width, B, with soil shear strength governed by the
Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion. The basic bearing capacity solutions also assume
vertical loading, a horizontal bearing surface, foundation depth less than the width, and
a horizontal ground surface. Methods to address other variations of these factors are
discussed in Section 5-3.3.

In most methods, the bearing capacity problem is simplified by replacing the soil above
the bearing elevation with an equivalent surcharge as shown in Figure 5-4(a). This
conservatively neglects the shear strength of the soil above the foundation depth.
Alternatively, Meyerhof (1951) assumed that the failure surface continued to the ground
surface and replaced the triangular wedge with equivalent stresses, p0 and s0.
Meyerhof’s geometry is shown in Figure 5-4(b). Basic formulations also assume that
the groundwater table is deeper than the failure zone.

                                                                       16 January 2025

distinct terms or superimposed sources of bearing resistance. The first term is
connected to the cohesion (or undrained shear strength) along the failure surface and
has a bearing capacity factor, Nc. The second term is related to the surcharge and has
a bearing capacity factor, Nq. The third term is related to the weight of the soil above
the failure surface and has a bearing capacity factor, Nγ.

4.4    Design Verification

As an important adjunct to design, a field verification program of load tests and in situ testing
must be developed and implemented through appropriate construction specification
requirements. A program should be specified, regardless of the contracting method.

A combination of load tests on aggregate columns constructed before, during, and after
production should be specified to verify the design assumptions and the performance
specification. There are three types of load tests: (1) short-term tests, which are used to
evaluate ultimate stone column bearing resistance, (2) long-term tests, which are used to
measure the consolidation settlement characteristics; and (3) horizontal or composite shear
tests, which are used to evaluate the composite aggregate-soil shear strength for use in

The short-term load tests, similar to pile load tests, should be performed after all excess pore
pressures induced during construction have been dissipated. The load increment should
closely correspond to the actual loading. For example, if the actual foundation load will be
applied very slowly, a load increment of approximately 10 percent of the ultimate should be
used. A rapid loading may result in immediate settlement, as well as consolidation
settlement. If the actual load will be applied rapidly, a load increment of 20 to 25 percent of
ultimate should be used. The tests are generally performed to 150% of the design load, and
the measured settlement is compared to project settlement tolerance. For example, a final
acceptance criterion of 1 inch of settlement at 150 to 200 percent of the design load appears
to be a reasonable criterion for columns supporting a structure.

results of short-term load tests on single stone columns. Mitchell (1981) reported that the

4-5.1.2         Overturning.

The stability of the wall for the failure mode of overturning can be determined by
defining a factor of safety equal to the restoring moment divided by the overturning
moment. The factor of safety, FOT, should be greater than or equal to 1.5.

An alternative method is to examine the location of the resultant, R, relative to the width
of the base of the wall. If R is in the middle one-third of the base for walls founded on
soil, the wall is considered safe. For walls founded on rock, R should be located in the
middle one-half of the base for the wall to be considered safe. 23

4-5.1.3         Sliding.

The stability of the wall for the failure mode of sliding is normally determined by using
horizontal force equilibrium. The factor of safety against sliding, FSL, is the ratio of the
resisting force to the horizontal earth pressure force. The resisting force is a
combination of the frictional resistance at the base of the wall and the adhesion
between the base of the wall and the soil foundation. For sliding resistance on fine-
grained soils, the adhesion should be multiplied by the effective width of the base (Be)
found using the uniform bearing pressure method. The factor of safety should be
greater than or equal to 1.5. The parameters used to calculate FSL are shown on Figure
4-27. If passive resistance is included, the minimum FSL should be increased to 2.0.
Minimum FSL may also need to be increased when base adhesion is included in the
resistance.

In some cases, a layer of coarse-grained soil may be placed below the wall as a bearing
material. Sliding should be checked at two locations. The shear resistance, Τ, should
be taken as the lowest of (1) the resistance at the interface between the base of the wall
and the bearing material and (2) the resistance within the clay using the full undrained
shear strength.
